metadata.title: Computable upper error bounds for Krylov approximations to matrix exponentials and associated phi-functions
metadata.authors: Tobias Jawecki, Winfried Auzinger, Othmar Koch

nodes.name: Approximation of the matrix exponential $\ee^{\sca t A}v$
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: We discuss the approximation of the matrix exponential, \begin{equation} E(t)v = \ee^{\sca\,t \Opgen} v, \quad \Opgen \in \C^{n\times n},~~\sca\in\C, \end{equation} with step size $ t $, applied to an initial vector $ v \in \C^n $. To simplify the notation we assume $ |\sca|=1 $ and $ \|v\|_2=1 $ without loss of generality.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $\ee^{\sca t A}v$ for a large matrix $A$, with $|\sca|=1$ and $\|v\|_2=1$ assumed w.l.o.g.

nodes.name: Nonexpansive case
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: We assume that $\mu_2(\sigma A)\leq 0$, where $\mu_2(\sigma A)$ denotes the logarithmic norm of $\sigma A$, or equivalently, $W(\sigma A)\subseteq \C_-$, where $W(\sigma A)$ denotes the field of values of $\sigma A$ and we will refer to this assumption as the \emph{nonexpansive case}. $\mu_2(\sigma A)\leq 0$ implies $\|E(t)\|_2\leq 1$ for $t\geq 0$. This is essentially a technical assumption, and most of our theoretical results carry over to a more general setting, in particular if a~priori information about $\mu_2(\sigma A)$ is available, such that $E(t)$ can be estimated as $\|E(t)\|_2 \leq \ee^{\mu_2(\sigma A)}$.
nodes.statement_short: The logarithmic norm satisfies $\mu_2(\sigma A)\le 0$, equivalently $W(\sigma A)\subseteq\C_-$, giving $\|E(t)\|_2\le 1$.

nodes.name: Conventional Krylov subspace $\Kry_m(\Opgen,v)$
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.origin_citation: Saad, Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems (2003)
nodes.statement: The numerical approximation of~\eqref{exp(itA)v} considered here (see~\eqref{Smv} below) is based on the conventional Krylov subspace \begin{equation*} \Kry_m(\Opgen,v) = \vecspan\{v,\Opgen v,\ldots,\Opgen^{m-1}v\} \subseteq \C^n. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Krylov identity (Arnoldi decomposition)
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: First, \tjnew{an orthonormal} basis of $ \Kry_m(\Opgen,v) $ is obtained by the well-known Arnoldi iteration, see~\cite{saad03}. This produces a basis matrix $ V_m \in \C^{n \times m} $ satisfying $ V_m^\ast\,V_m = I_{m \times m} $, and an upper Hessenberg matrix $ T_m \in \C^{m\times m} $ such that the Krylov identity\footnote{ Here, $ {e_m = (0,\ldots,0,1)^\ast \in \C^m} $, and in the sequel we also denote $ {e_1 = (1,0,\ldots,0)^\ast \in \C^m} $.} \begin{equation} \Opgen\,V_m = V_m T_m + \tau_{m+1,m}\,v_{m+1}e_m^\ast \end{equation} is valid, with $\tau_{m+1,m}\in\R_+$ and $v_{m+1}\in\C^n$ with $\|v_{m+1}\|_2=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Arnoldi produces orthonormal $V_m$ and upper Hessenberg $T_m$ with $AV_m=V_mT_m+\tau_{m+1,m}v_{m+1}e_m^*$.
assumptions: First, \tjnew{an orthonormal} basis of $ \Kry_m(\Opgen,v) $ is obtained by the well-known Arnoldi iteration, see~\cite{saad03}.
conclusions: This produces a basis matrix $ V_m \in \C^{n \times m} $ satisfying $ V_m^\ast\,V_m = I_{m \times m} $, and an upper Hessenberg matrix $ T_m \in \C^{m\times m} $ such that the Krylov identity\footnote{ Here, $ {e_m = (0,\ldots,0,1)^\ast \in \C^m} $, and in the sequel we also denote $ {e_1 = (1,0,\ldots,0)^\ast \in \C^m} $.} \begin{equation} \Opgen\,V_m = V_m T_m + \tau_{m+1,m}\,v_{m+1}e_m^\ast \end{equation} is valid, with $\tau_{m+1,m}\in\R_+$ and $v_{m+1}\in\C^n$ with $\|v_{m+1}\|_2=1$.

nodes.name: Lucky breakdown of the Arnoldi iteration
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: We are assuming that the Arnoldi iteration is executed until the desired dimension~$ m $. Then, by construction, all lower diagonal entries of $ T_m $ are positive~\cite{saad03}. If this is not the case, i.e., if a breakdown occurs, it is known that this breakdown is {\em lucky,}, i.e., the approximation~\eqref{Smv} below obtained in the step before breakdown is already exact, see~\cite{saad92s}.
nodes.statement_short: If Arnoldi breaks down before dimension $m$ the breakdown is lucky: the previous approximation is already exact.

nodes.name: Identities from the upper Hessenberg structure of $T_m$
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: The following identities hold true due to the upper Hessenberg [tridiagonal] structure of~$ T_m $ together with~\eqref{krylovidentity}: \begin{equation} e_m^\ast\,T_m^{j}\,e_1 = 0 \quad \text{for}~~ j=0,\ldots,m-2, \end{equation} and \tjnew{ \begin{equation} \Opgen^{j}v = V_m T_m^{j} e_1,~~~0\leq j \leq m-1, \end{equation} see for instance~\cite[Theorem 2]{DK89} or~\cite{saad92s}.}
nodes.statement_short: Hessenberg structure gives $e_m^*T_m^je_1=0$ for $j\le m-2$ and $A^jv=V_mT_m^je_1$ for $j\le m-1$.
assumptions: the upper Hessenberg [tridiagonal] structure of~$ T_m $ together with~\eqref{krylovidentity}

nodes.name: $\gamma_m$
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: Furthermore, let \begin{equation} \gamma_m = e_m^\ast\,T_m^{m-1} e_1 = \prod_{j=1}^{m-1} (T_m)_{j+1,j}\,, \end{equation} where the claimed identity also follows from the upper Hessenberg [tridiagonal] structure of~$ T_m $.

nodes.name: Standard Krylov approximation $S_m(t)v$
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: The standard Krylov approximation to $ E(t)v $ is \begin{equation} S_m(t)v = V_m\,\ee^{\sca\,t T_m}\,V_m^\ast\,v = V_m\,\ee^{\sca\,t T_m}e_1. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Error operator $L_m(t)$
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: We denote the corresponding error operator by $ L_m(t) $, with \begin{equation} L_m(t)=E(t)-S_m(t) \in \C^{n \times n}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Defect operator $D_m(t)$
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: We define the \emph{defect}\, operator $ D_m(t) $ of $ S_m(t) $ by \begin{equation*} D_m(t) = \sca\,\Opgen\,S_m(t) - S_m'(t) \in \C^{n \times n}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Defect-based integral representation of the approximation error
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: Then, $ L_m(t)v $ and $ D_m(t)v $ are related via the differential equation \begin{equation*} L_m'(t)v = \sca\,\Opgen\,L_m(t)v + D_m(t)v, \quad L_m(0)v=0, \end{equation*} whence \begin{equation} L_m(t)v = \int_0^t E(t-s)\,D_m(s)v\,\dd s. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The error solves an inhomogeneous ODE driven by the defect, hence $L_m(t)v=\int_0^t E(t-s)D_m(s)v\,\dd s$.

nodes.name: Explicit representation of the defect $D_m(s)v$
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: An explicit representation for $ D_m(s)v $ is obtained from~\eqref{krylovidentity}, \begin{align} D_m(s)v &= \sca\,\Opgen\,V_m\,\ee^{\sca\,s\,T_m}e_1 - \sca\,V_m T_m\,\ee^{\sca\,s\,T_m}e_1 = \sca\,(\Opgen\,V_m - V_m T_m)\,\ee^{\sca\,s\,T_m}e_1 \notag \\ &= \sca \tau_{m+1,m}\,\big(e_m^\ast\,\ee^{\sca\,s\,T_m}e_1\big)\,v_{m+1}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The defect is a scalar multiple of the next Krylov vector: $D_m(s)v=\sca\tau_{m+1,m}(e_m^*\ee^{\sca sT_m}e_1)v_{m+1}$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic order of the defect and of the error
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: Asymptotically for $ t \to 0 $, \begin{equation} D_m(t)v = \sca \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\frac{(\sigma t)^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,v_{m+1} + {\mathcal{O}}(t^m), \end{equation} which follows from the Taylor series representation for $ \ee^{\sca\,t\,T_m} $ together with~\eqref{eTe} and~\eqref{gammam}. \tjnew{Thus, by~\eqref{LDint} and~\eqref{Dm-lead} we obtain \begin{equation} \| D_m(t)v \| = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m-1}), \quad \text{and} \quad \| L_m(t)v \| = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m}). \end{equation}}
nodes.statement_short: For $t\to0$ the defect is $\mathcal{O}(t^{m-1})$ and the error $\mathcal{O}(t^m)$.

nodes.name: Asymptotically leading term of the Krylov error
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: For any $ A \in \C^{\tjnew{n \times n}} $ the error $ L_m(t)v $ satisfies the asymptotic relation \begin{equation} L_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{(\sca\,t)^{m}}{m!}v_{m+1} + R_{m+1}(t), \quad R_{m+1}(t) = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}), \end{equation} for $ t \to 0 $.
nodes.statement_short: The leading error term is $\tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m(\sca t)^m/m!\;v_{m+1}$, with remainder $\mathcal{O}(t^{m+1})$.

nodes.name: Proof of the asymptotically leading error term
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: Taylor expansion. Due to $ L_m(t)v = {\mathcal{O}}(t^m) $, \tjnew{see~\eqref{orderofDmLm},} \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &L_m(t)v = E(t)v - S_m(t)v = \frac{(\sca\,t)^m}{{m!}}(\Opgen^m v - V_m T_m^m\,e_1) + R_{m+1}(t),\\ &\text{with Taylor remainder}~~ R_{m+1}(t) = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}). \end{aligned} \end{equation} Multiplying the identity~\tjnew{{\eqref{HVTm}} (with $ j = m-1 $) by $ A $} and using~\eqref{krylovidentity} gives \begin{align*} \Opgen^m\,v &= \Opgen\,V_m T_m^{m-1} e_1 = (V_m T_m + \tau_{m+1,m}\,v_{m+1} e_m^\ast) T_m^{m-1} e_1 \\ &= V_m T_m^m\,e_1 + \tau_{m+1,m}\, (e_m^\ast\,T_m^{m-1} e_1)\,v_{m+1} = V_m T_m^m\,e_1 + \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m v_{m+1}, \end{align*} whence~\eqref{prop-3-proof} simplifies to~\eqref{asy-leading}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Taylor expansion of $E(t)v-S_m(t)v$ to order $m$, then evaluate $A^mv-V_mT_m^me_1$ with the Krylov identity.

nodes.name: Taylor expansion of the error
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: Taylor expansion. Due to $ L_m(t)v = {\mathcal{O}}(t^m) $, \tjnew{see~\eqref{orderofDmLm},} \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &L_m(t)v = E(t)v - S_m(t)v = \frac{(\sca\,t)^m}{{m!}}(\Opgen^m v - V_m T_m^m\,e_1) + R_{m+1}(t),\\ &\text{with Taylor remainder}~~ R_{m+1}(t) = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}). \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Expand $L_m(t)v$ to order $m$ using that the error is $\mathcal{O}(t^m)$.

nodes.name: Evaluate $A^m v$ via the Krylov identity
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: Multiplying the identity~\tjnew{{\eqref{HVTm}} (with $ j = m-1 $) by $ A $} and using~\eqref{krylovidentity} gives \begin{align*} \Opgen^m\,v &= \Opgen\,V_m T_m^{m-1} e_1 = (V_m T_m + \tau_{m+1,m}\,v_{m+1} e_m^\ast) T_m^{m-1} e_1 \\ &= V_m T_m^m\,e_1 + \tau_{m+1,m}\, (e_m^\ast\,T_m^{m-1} e_1)\,v_{m+1} = V_m T_m^m\,e_1 + \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m v_{m+1}, \end{align*} whence~\eqref{prop-3-proof} simplifies to~\eqref{asy-leading}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Multiply $A^{m-1}v=V_mT_m^{m-1}e_1$ by $A$ and apply the Krylov identity to isolate $\tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m v_{m+1}$.

nodes.name: Explicit form of the Taylor remainder $R_{m+1}$
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement: The Taylor remainder $ R_{m+1} $ in~\eqref{asy-leading} can be specified in a more explicit way showing its dependence on~$ m $, $$ R_{m+1}(t) = \frac{(\sigma\,t)^{m+1}}{m!} \int_{0}^{1} \big(A^{m+1} \ee^{\sigma\,\theta\,t\,A} v - V_m T_m^{m+1}\ee^{\sigma\,\theta\,t\,T_m} e_1 \big){(1-\theta)}^m\,\dd\theta . $$
nodes.statement_short: The remainder has an explicit integral form exhibiting its dependence on $m$.

nodes.name: Integral bound for the error in terms of the defect
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: For the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} we have $\| E(t-s) \|_2 \leq 1$ for $0\leq s \leq t$, and~\eqref{LDint} implies \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 = \Big\| \int_0^t E(t-s)\,D_m(s)v\,\dd s\ \Big\|_2 \leq \int_0^t \|D_m(s)v\|_2\,\dd s. \end{equation*} With $\|v_{m+1}\|_2 = 1$, and \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \delta_m(s) = e_m^\ast\,\ee^{\sca\,s\,T_m}e_1 = \big( \ee^{\sca\,s\,T_m} \big)_{m,1}, \end{equation} together with~\eqref{Dm(s)v} we obtain \begin{equation} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)| \, \dd s. \end{equation} \end{subequations} This estimate is also given in~\cite[Section~III.2]{lubich08}.
nodes.statement_short: Nonexpansivity turns the integral representation into $\|L_m(t)v\|_2\le\tau_{m+1,m}\int_0^t|\delta_m(s)|\dd s$.
assumptions: For the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} we have $\| E(t-s) \|_2 \leq 1$ for $0\leq s \leq t$

nodes.name: $\delta_m(s)$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: \delta_m(s) = e_m^\ast\,\ee^{\sca\,s\,T_m}e_1 = \big( \ee^{\sca\,s\,T_m} \big)_{m,1},

nodes.name: Hermite interpolation of the exponential on the spectrum of $T_m$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: To approximate the error integral in~\eqref{errorapprox1} we use the representation of matrix exponentials via Hermite interpolation of the scalar exponential function on the spectrum of the matrix~$ T_m $, see~\cite[Chap.~1]{higham08}: If $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r$ ($ r \leq m $) denote the distinct eigenvalues of~$ T_m $ and $ n_j $ is the dimension of the largest Jordan block associated with~$ \mu_j $, then \begin{equation} \ee^{\sca\,t T_m} = p_t(T_m), \end{equation} where $ p_t(\lambda) $ is the {Hermite} interpolant of degree $ \leq m-1 $ of the function \begin{equation} {f_t}(\lambda) = \ee^{\sca\,t\lambda} \end{equation} over the nodes $ \mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m $ in the sense of~\cite[(1.7)]{higham08}, \begin{equation*} p_t^{(\ell)}(\mu_j) = f_t^{(\ell)}(\mu_j), \quad j=1,\ldots,r, \quad \ell=0,\ldots,n_j-1. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: $\ee^{\sca tT_m}=p_t(T_m)$ where $p_t$ Hermite-interpolates $f_t(\lambda)=\ee^{\sca t\lambda}$ on $\mathrm{spec}(T_m)$.
assumptions: If $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r$ ($ r \leq m $) denote the distinct eigenvalues of~$ T_m $ and $ n_j $ is the dimension of the largest Jordan block associated with~$ \mu_j $

nodes.name: Degree of the Hermite interpolant $p_t$ is exactly $m-1$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: \wa{For a general matrix, the degree of $ p_t $ may be smaller than $ m-1 $. However, in our context a special case occurs: Since the lower diagonal entries of $ T_m $ do not vanish, $ T_m $ is nonderogatory, i.e., for each eigenvalue $ \mu_j $ the associated eigenspace is one-dimensional, see~\cite[Section~3.1]{horn85}. Then, $ \sum_{j=1}^{r} n_j = m $, which implies that the degree of $ p_t $ is exactly $ m-1 $.}
assumptions: Since the lower diagonal entries of $ T_m $ do not vanish, $ T_m $ is nonderogatory, i.e., for each eigenvalue $ \mu_j $ the associated eigenspace is one-dimensional, see~\cite[Section~3.1]{horn85}.
conclusions: Then, $ \sum_{j=1}^{r} n_j = m $, which implies that the degree of $ p_t $ is exactly $ m-1 $.

nodes.name: Spectral inclusion $\text{spec}(\sca T_m)\subseteq\C_-$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: By applying basic properties of the Krylov decomposition and imposed conditions on the numerical range of $\Opgen$ we obtain \begin{equation} \text{spec}(\sca\,T_m) \subseteq W(\sca\,T_m) \subseteq W(\sca\,\Opgen) \subseteq \C_-. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Representation and estimate of $\delta_m(t)$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: Let $T_m \in \C^{m\times m}$ be an upper Hessenberg matrix with eigenvalues $ \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m $ and $ \text{spec}(\sca T_m) \subseteq \C_- $. Then the function $ \delta_m(t) $ defined as in~\eqref{defdelta}, i.e., \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = e_m^\ast\,\ee^{\sca\,t\,T_m}e_1 = \big( \ee^{\sca\,t\,T_m} \big)_{m,1}, \end{equation*} satisfies \begin{equation} \delta_m(t) = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m \leq {\frac{t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,\gamma_m,} \end{equation} with $ \gamma_m $ from~\eqref{gammam} and where $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t}$ is the {$ (m-1) $-th} divided difference over $ \text{\rm spec}(T_m) $ of the function $ f_t $ defined in~\eqref{def:thetadd}.
nodes.statement_short: $\delta_m(t)$ equals $\gamma_m$ times the $(m-1)$-st divided difference of $f_t$ over $\mathrm{spec}(T_m)$, bounded by $t^{m-1}\gamma_m/(m-1)!$.
assumptions: Let $T_m \in \C^{m\times m}$ be an upper Hessenberg matrix with eigenvalues $ \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m $ and $ \text{spec}(\sca T_m) \subseteq \C_- $.

nodes.name: Proof of the representation and estimate of $\delta_m(t)$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: We proceed from the Newton representation of the interpolant $p_t(\lambda) $ from~\eqref{pt}, \begin{equation*} p_t(\lambda) = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{j+1}}{f_t}\,\omega_j(\lambda), \end{equation*} with $ \omega_j(\lambda) = (\lambda-\lambda_1) \cdots (\lambda-\lambda_{j}) $. {From~\eqref{eTe} and by definition of $ \gamma_m $, it is obvious that the $ \omega_j $ satisfy} \begin{equation*} e_m^\ast\,\omega_j(T_m)\,e_1 = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0, & j=0,\ldots,m-2, \\ \gamma_m,& j=m-1. \end{array}\right. \end{equation*} Together with~\eqref{pt} this shows that the identity claimed in~\eqref{deltam-repr} is valid: \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = e_m^\ast\,\ee^{\sca\,t T_m}\,e_1 = e_m^\ast\,p_t(T_m) e_1 = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{j+1}}{f_t} e_m^\ast\,\omega_j(T_m)e_1 = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m. \end{equation*} According to~\cite[(B.28)]{higham08} the divided difference can be estimated by \begin{align*} &|f_t[\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m]| \leq \frac{\max_{z \in \Omega} D^{(m-1)}f_t(z)}{(m-1)!}\\ &\text{for convex $\Omega \subseteq \C$ which contains all eigenvalues $ \lambda_j$.} \end{align*} With $D^{(m-1)}f_t(\lambda) = (\sca\,t)^{m-1} \ee^{\sca\,t\lambda} $, $ |\sca|=1 $ and $\text{Re}(\sca \lambda_j)\leq 0$ we obtain \begin{equation*} |\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t}| \leq \frac{t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}, \end{equation*} which implies the estimate~\eqref{deltam-repr} for $ \delta_m(t) $. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Newton form of the Hermite interpolant kills all but the top divided difference; then bound it by Higham's convex-hull estimate.

nodes.name: Newton representation of the interpolant
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: We proceed from the Newton representation of the interpolant $p_t(\lambda) $ from~\eqref{pt}, \begin{equation*} p_t(\lambda) = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{j+1}}{f_t}\,\omega_j(\lambda), \end{equation*} with $ \omega_j(\lambda) = (\lambda-\lambda_1) \cdots (\lambda-\lambda_{j}) $. {From~\eqref{eTe} and by definition of $ \gamma_m $, it is obvious that the $ \omega_j $ satisfy} \begin{equation*} e_m^\ast\,\omega_j(T_m)\,e_1 = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0, & j=0,\ldots,m-2, \\ \gamma_m,& j=m-1. \end{array}\right. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $p_t$ in Newton form and evaluate $e_m^*\omega_j(T_m)e_1$, which vanishes except for $j=m-1$.

nodes.name: Derive the identity for $\delta_m(t)$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: Together with~\eqref{pt} this shows that the identity claimed in~\eqref{deltam-repr} is valid: \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = e_m^\ast\,\ee^{\sca\,t T_m}\,e_1 = e_m^\ast\,p_t(T_m) e_1 = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{j+1}}{f_t} e_m^\ast\,\omega_j(T_m)e_1 = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Only the top Newton term survives, giving $\delta_m(t)=f_t[\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m]\gamma_m$.

nodes.name: Bound the divided difference
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: According to~\cite[(B.28)]{higham08} the divided difference can be estimated by \begin{align*} &|f_t[\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m]| \leq \frac{\max_{z \in \Omega} D^{(m-1)}f_t(z)}{(m-1)!}\\ &\text{for convex $\Omega \subseteq \C$ which contains all eigenvalues $ \lambda_j$.} \end{align*} With $D^{(m-1)}f_t(\lambda) = (\sca\,t)^{m-1} \ee^{\sca\,t\lambda} $, $ |\sca|=1 $ and $\text{Re}(\sca \lambda_j)\leq 0$ we obtain \begin{equation*} |\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t}| \leq \frac{t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}, \end{equation*} which implies the estimate~\eqref{deltam-repr} for $ \delta_m(t) $. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Apply Higham's convex-hull bound with $|\sca|=1$ and $\mathrm{Re}(\sca\lambda_j)\le0$ to get $t^{m-1}/(m-1)!$.

nodes.name: Computable upper bound
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: For the nonexpansive case the error $ L_m(t)v $ of the Krylov approximation~\eqref{Smv} to $ E(t)v $ satisfies \begin{equation} \| L_m(t)v \|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{t^{m}}{m!} \end{equation} with $ \tau_{m+1,m} $ from~\eqref{krylovidentity} and $ \gamma_m $ from~\eqref{gammam}.
nodes.statement_short: In the nonexpansive case the Krylov error obeys the computable bound $\tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m t^m/m!$.
assumptions: For the nonexpansive case the error $ L_m(t)v $ of the Krylov approximation~\eqref{Smv} to $ E(t)v $

nodes.name: Proof of the computable upper bound
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: We proceed from~\eqref{errestintdefect}. For $ \delta_m $ defined in~\eqref{defdelta}, Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} implies \begin{equation*} |\delta_m(s)| \leq \frac{s^{m-1}}{(m-1)!} \gamma_m, \end{equation*} and this gives an upper bound for the error integral~\eqref{errorapprox1}: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m \int_0^t \frac{s^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,\dd s = \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m \frac{t^{m}}{m!}, \end{equation*} which completes the proof. \tjnew{ Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} is applied here in the nonexpansive case ($ W(\sigma A) \subseteq \C_- $) which implies the requirement $ \text{spec}(\sca T_m) \subseteq \C_- $, see~\eqref{subsetofspectrum}.} \qed
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|\delta_m(s)|$ by Proposition 3.1 and integrate the resulting monomial over $[0,t]$.

nodes.name: Bound the defect scalar
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: For $ \delta_m $ defined in~\eqref{defdelta}, Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} implies \begin{equation*} |\delta_m(s)| \leq \frac{s^{m-1}}{(m-1)!} \gamma_m, \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 3.1 to bound $|\delta_m(s)|$ by $s^{m-1}\gamma_m/(m-1)!$.

nodes.name: Integrate the bound over $[0,t]$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: and this gives an upper bound for the error integral~\eqref{errorapprox1}: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m \int_0^t \frac{s^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,\dd s = \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m \frac{t^{m}}{m!}, \end{equation*} which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the monomial bound to obtain $\tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m t^m/m!$.

nodes.name: Error estimate $\Era$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: We denote the error estimate given by~\eqref{asyerrest} as \begin{equation}\tag{$\Era$} \Era = \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{t^{m}}{m!}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Asymptotical correctness
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: The upper bound~\eqref{asyerrest} is asymptotically correct for $ t \to 0 $, i.e., \begin{equation} \| L_m(t)v \|_2 = \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{t^m}{m!} + {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The deviation of the bound from the true error is $\mathcal{O}(t^{m+1})$, of higher order than the error itself.
assumptions: The upper bound~\eqref{asyerrest} is asymptotically correct for $ t \to 0 $

nodes.name: Proof of asymptotical correctness
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: The asymptotic estimate \begin{align*} \bigg| \| L_m(t)v \|_2 - \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{t^m}{m!} \bigg| &= \bigg| \| L_m(t)v \|_2 - \Big\| \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{(\sca\,t)^{m}}{m!}v_{m+1} \Big\|_2 \bigg| \\ &\leq \Big\| L_m(t)v - \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{(\sca\,t)^{m}}{m!}v_{m+1} \Big\|_2 = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}) \end{align*} is valid due to~Proposition~\ref{prop:prop3}, and this proves~\eqref{asyerrcorr}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Reverse triangle inequality plus the $\mathcal{O}(t^{m+1})$ remainder of Proposition 2.1.

nodes.name: Shift-and-invert Krylov approximation
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: In \cite[Section 4]{eshhoc06} a defect-based error formulation is given for the shift-and-invert Krylov approximation of the matrix exponential function. In contrast to the standard Krylov method, the defect is not of order $m-1$ for $t\to 0$ there. Hence, our new results do not directly apply to shift-and-invert Krylov approximations. A study of a posteriori error estimates for the shift-and-invert approach is a topic of future investigations.
nodes.statement_short: For shift-and-invert Krylov the defect is not of order $m-1$, so the new results do not carry over.

nodes.name: A posteriori error estimates for the shift-and-invert approach
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound for the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: A study of a posteriori error estimates for the shift-and-invert approach is a topic of future investigations.

nodes.name: $\phif$-functions
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to phi-functions
nodes.statement: As another application we consider the so-called $ \phif $-functions, with power series representation \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \phif_p(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{z^k}{(k+p)!}, \quad p\geq 0. \end{equation} We have $ \phif_0(z) = \ee^z $, and \begin{equation} \phif_p(z) = \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1}\ee^{\theta z}\,\dd\theta, \quad p \geq 1. \end{equation} \end{subequations}
nodes.statement_short: $\phif_p(z)=\sum_{k\ge0} z^k/(k+p)!$, with $\phif_0=\ee^z$ and an integral representation for $p\ge1$.

nodes.name: Krylov approximation to $\phif$-functions
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to phi-functions
nodes.statement: Krylov approximation is a common technique to evaluate $\phif$-functions of matrices applied to a starting vector, \begin{equation} \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v \approx V_m \phif_p(\sca\,t T_m) e_1,~~~~p\geq 0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Error $L^p_m(t)v$ of the Krylov approximation to $\phif_p$
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to phi-functions
nodes.statement: We use the following notation for the error in the $\phif$-functions: \begin{equation} L^p_m(t)v = \phif_p(\sca\,t\,\Opgen)v - V_m \phif_p(\sca\,t\,T_m) e_1. \end{equation} With~\eqref{generalizeerrornotation} we generalize the previously used notation: $ L_m(t) = L^0_m(t) $.

nodes.name: Upper bound for Krylov approximations to $\phif$-functions
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to phi-functions
nodes.statement: The error of the Krylov approximation~\eqref{kry-phi} to $ \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v $ with $ p \geq 0 $ satisfies \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} L^p_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m \frac{(\sca\, t)^m}{(m+p)!} \, v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}). \end{equation} Furthermore, \tjnew{in the nonexpansive case} its norm is bounded by \begin{equation} \|L^p_m(t)v \|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^{m}}{(m+p)!}, \end{equation} \end{subequations} and this bound is asymptotically correct for $ t \to 0 $.
nodes.statement_short: The $\phif_p$ Krylov error has leading term $\tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m(\sca t)^m/(m+p)!$ and, in the nonexpansive case, is bounded by $\tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m t^m/(m+p)!$.
assumptions: The error of the Krylov approximation~\eqref{kry-phi} to $ \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v $ with $ p \geq 0 $

nodes.name: Proof of the upper bound for $\phif$-functions
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to phi-functions
nodes.statement: For $p=0$ the result directly follows from Propositions~\ref{prop:prop3},~\ref{prop:prop4} and Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp}. We now assume $ p \geq 1 $. Via the series representation~\eqref{defphiseries} of $\phif_p$ we can determine the leading term of the error in an analogous way as in Proposition~\ref{prop:prop3}: \begin{align*} \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v - V_m \phif_p(\sca\,t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{(\sca\,t)^m \,(A^m v - V_m T_m^m e_1)}{(m+p)!} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}) \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m \frac{(\sca\, t)^m}{(m+p)!} \, v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}), \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{leadingtermphij}. Furthermore, proceeding from~\eqref{defphiint} we obtain \begin{align*} \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v - V_m \phif_p(\sca\,t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1}\big( \ee^{\sca\,\theta\,t \Opgen} v - V_m\,\ee^{\sca\,\theta\,t T_m} e_1 \big) \,\dd \theta\\ &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} L_m(\theta\,t)v \,\dd \theta, \end{align*} with the error $L_m(t)v$ for the matrix exponential case. Now we apply Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp} to obtain \begin{align*} \| \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v - V_m \phif_p(\sca\,t T_m) e_1 \|_2 &\leq \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\dd \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^m}{(p-1)!\,m!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^m \,\dd \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^{m}}{(m+p)!}, \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{eresphij}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Series expansion gives the leading term; the integral representation of $\phif_p$ combined with Theorem 3.1 gives the bound.

nodes.name: Reduce the case $p=0$
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to phi-functions
nodes.statement: For $p=0$ the result directly follows from Propositions~\ref{prop:prop3},~\ref{prop:prop4} and Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp}. We now assume $ p \geq 1 $.
nodes.statement_short: For $p=0$ the claim is the exponential case already proved; assume $p\ge1$.

nodes.name: Leading term from the series representation
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to phi-functions
nodes.statement: Via the series representation~\eqref{defphiseries} of $\phif_p$ we can determine the leading term of the error in an analogous way as in Proposition~\ref{prop:prop3}: \begin{align*} \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v - V_m \phif_p(\sca\,t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{(\sca\,t)^m \,(A^m v - V_m T_m^m e_1)}{(m+p)!} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}) \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m \frac{(\sca\, t)^m}{(m+p)!} \, v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}), \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{leadingtermphij}.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\phif_p$ in its power series and reuse the computation of $A^mv-V_mT_m^me_1$.

nodes.name: Bound via the integral representation
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to phi-functions
nodes.statement: Furthermore, proceeding from~\eqref{defphiint} we obtain \begin{align*} \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v - V_m \phif_p(\sca\,t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1}\big( \ee^{\sca\,\theta\,t \Opgen} v - V_m\,\ee^{\sca\,\theta\,t T_m} e_1 \big) \,\dd \theta\\ &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} L_m(\theta\,t)v \,\dd \theta, \end{align*} with the error $L_m(t)v$ for the matrix exponential case. Now we apply Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp} to obtain \begin{align*} \| \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v - V_m \phif_p(\sca\,t T_m) e_1 \|_2 &\leq \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\dd \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^m}{(p-1)!\,m!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^m \,\dd \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^{m}}{(m+p)!}, \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{eresphij}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Write $L^p_m$ as a $\theta$-integral of $L_m(\theta t)v$, apply Theorem 3.1 and evaluate the Beta integral.

nodes.name: Saad's error representation
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: With the $\phif$-functions defined in~\eqref{defphi}, the error~\eqref{Lerror} can be represented in the form \begin{align} L_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\,\sca\,t \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} e_m^\ast\phif_{j}(\sca\,tT_m)\,e_1 (\sca\,t \Opgen)^{j-1}v_{m+1}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The Krylov error expands as an infinite series in $\phif_j(\sca tT_m)$ weighted by powers of $\sca tA$ applied to $v_{m+1}$.

nodes.name: Error estimate $\Erone$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: Analogously to~\cite[Section 5.2]{saad92s} we use the notation $\Erone$ for the norm of this term, \begin{equation}\tag{$\Erone$} \Erone = \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,|e_m^\ast\phif_1(\sca\,t T_m)e_1|. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Computation of $\phif_1(\sca t T_m)$ via the extended matrix $\Tcor_m$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: According to~\cite[Proposition~2.1]{saad92s}, $\phif_1(\sca\,t T_m)$ can be computed from the extended matrix \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \Tcor_m = \begin{bmatrix} T_m&0\\ \tau_{m+1,m}\,e_m^\ast&0 \end{bmatrix}\in\C^{(m+1)\times (m+1)} \end{equation} as \begin{equation} \ee^{\sca\,t\Tcor_m} e_1= \begin{bmatrix} \ee^{\sca\,tT_m}e_1\\ \tau_{m+1,m}\,\sca\,t \,(e_m^\ast\,\phif_1(\sca\,t T_m)\,e_1) \end{bmatrix}\in\C^{m+1}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}
nodes.statement_short: Exponentiating the $(m+1)\times(m+1)$ extended matrix $\Tcor_m$ yields $e_m^*\phif_1(\sca tT_m)e_1$ as its last entry.

nodes.name: Corrected Krylov approximation $\Scor_m(t)v$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: Equation~\eqref{computephi1} can be used to evaluate the error estimate $\Erone$ or a corrected Krylov approximation in the form \begin{equation} \Scor_m(t)v = \Vcor_m\,\ee^{\sca\,t\Tcor_m}e_1 \text{~~~with~~~} \Vcor_m=\Big[ V_m\,\big|\,v_{m+1} \Big] \in\C^{n\times (m+1)}, \end{equation} for which the first term of the error expansion according to Proposition~\ref{prop:saad92} vanishes, see~\cite{saad92s}. For the error of the corrected Krylov approximation we use the notation \begin{equation*} L_m^+(t)v = E(t)v - \Scor_m(t)v. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The corrected approximation appends $v_{m+1}$ to the basis and uses $\ee^{\sca t\Tcor_m}e_1$, cancelling the first error term.

nodes.name: Corrected Krylov approximation to $\phif_p$ and its error $L^{p,+}_m$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: The corrected Krylov approximation to $\phif_p(\sca\,t\,\Opgen)v$ is given in~\cite[Theorem 2]{sidje98}: \begin{equation*} \phif_p(\sca\,t\,\Opgen)v \approx \Vcor_m \phif_p(\sca\,t\,\Tcor_m) e_1 \end{equation*} with $\Tcor_m$ and $\Vcor_m$ given in~\eqref{definetcor} and~\eqref{Smbar}. The error of the corrected Krylov approximation is denoted by \begin{equation} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \phif_p(\sca\,t\,\Opgen)v - \Vcor_m \phif_p(\sca\,t\,\Tcor_m) e_1. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Error representation for standard and corrected Krylov approximations to $\phif_p$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: The error of the Krylov approximation $L^p_m(t)v$, see~\eqref{generalizeerrornotation}, satisfies \begin{equation} L^p_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} \sca\,t \sum_{j=p+1}^{\infty} (e_m^\ast \phif_j(\sca\,t\,T_m) e_1) \,(\sca\,t\,\Opgen)^{j-p-1} v_{m+1}. \end{equation} The error of the corrected Krylov approximation $L^{p,+}_m(t)v$, see~\eqref{generalizeerrornotation2}, is given by \begin{equation} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} \sca\,t \sum_{j=p+2}^{\infty} (e_m^\ast \phif_j(\sca\,t\,T_m) e_1) \,(\sca\,t\,\Opgen)^{j-p-1} v_{m+1}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}
nodes.statement_short: Both the standard and the corrected $\phif_p$ errors are series in $\phif_j(\sca tT_m)$, starting at $j=p+1$ resp. $j=p+2$.

nodes.name: Asymptotically leading terms and the $\Erone$ estimators for $\phif$-functions
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: From the representation~\eqref{defphiseries} for the $\phif_j$ together with~\eqref{eTe} and~\eqref{gammam} we observe \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} e_m^\ast \phif_j(\sca t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{(\sca t)^{m-1} e_m^\ast T_m^{m-1}\,e_1}{(m-1+j)!} + \mathcal{O}(t^m) = \gamma_m \,\frac{(\sca t)^{m-1}}{(m-1+j)!} + \mathcal{O}(t^m). \end{aligned} \end{equation} By~\eqref{em-phi-e1} we observe $ e_m^\ast\phif_{j}(\sca\,tT_m)\,e_1 = \mathcal{O}(t^{m-1}) $ for $ j \geq 0 $ and we conclude that the asymptotically leading order term of $ L^p_m(t)v $ for $ t \to 0 $ is obtained by the leading term ($j=p+1$) of the series~\eqref{generalizeerrorSaadsum1}: \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} L^p_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} \sca\,t (e_m^\ast \phif_{p+1}(\sca\,t\,T_m) e_1 ) v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^m). \end{equation} Analogously we obtain the asymptotically leading order term of $ L^{p,+}_m(t)v $ for $ t \to 0 $ by the leading term ($j=p+2$) of the series~\eqref{generalizeerrorSaadsum2}: \begin{equation} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} (\sca\,t)^2 (e_m^\ast \phif_{p+2}(\sca\,t\,T_m) e_1) \,\Opgen v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}). \end{equation} \end{subequations} The asymptotically leading terms in~\eqref{Lpleadingtermsum} and~\eqref{Lpplusleadingtermsum} can be used as error estimators: \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \|L^p_m(t)v\|_2 \approx \tau_{m+1,m}\,t |e_m^\ast \phif_{p+1}(\sca\,t\,T_m) e_1| \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \approx \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2 |e_m^\ast \phif_{p+2}(\sca\,t\,T_m) e_1|. \end{equation} \end{subequations} The error estimators~\eqref{LPnextphierrorest} and~\eqref{LPplusnextphierrorest} are already suggested in \cite{sidje98,niewri12}. We will refer to them as $\Erone$ in the context of the $\phif$-functions with standard and corrected Krylov approximation, generalizing the corresponding quantities for the exponential case $p=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $e_m^*\phif_j(\sca tT_m)e_1=\mathcal{O}(t^{m-1})$, the $j=p+1$ (resp. $j=p+2$) term dominates and yields the $\Erone$ estimators.

nodes.name: Upper bound for the corrected Krylov approximation
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: The error of the corrected Krylov approximation~\eqref{generalizeerrornotation2} to $ \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v $ with $ p \geq 0 $ satisfies \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m \frac{(\sca\, t)^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!} \, \Opgen v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+2}). \end{equation} Furthermore, \tjnew{in the nonexpansive case} its norm is bounded by \begin{equation} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2\, \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m \frac{t^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!}, \end{equation} \end{subequations} and this bound is asymptotically correct for $ t \to 0 $.
nodes.statement_short: The corrected $\phif_p$ error is $\mathcal{O}(t^{m+1})$ with explicit leading term and, in the nonexpansive case, bounded by $\|Av_{m+1}\|_2\tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m t^{m+1}/(m+p+1)!$.
assumptions: The error of the corrected Krylov approximation~\eqref{generalizeerrornotation2} to $ \phif_p(\sca\,t \Opgen)v $ with $ p \geq 0 $

nodes.name: Proof of the upper bound for the corrected Krylov approximation
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: Applying~\eqref{em-phi-e1} (with $j=p+2$) to~\eqref{Lpplusleadingtermsum} shows~\eqref{leadingtermphijcor}: \begin{equation*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\, \gamma_m\, \frac{(\sca\,t)^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!} \,\Opgen v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+2}). \end{equation*} From Proposition~\ref{prop:generalSaadsum} we observe \begin{align*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \sigma\,t\,\Opgen \,\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v. \end{align*} Using the integral representation analogously as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi} for $L^{p+1}_m(t)v$ and formula~\eqref{LDint} for $L_m(t)v$, we obtain \begin{align*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v &= \sigma\,t\,\Opgen\,\, L^{p+1}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \Opgen\, L_m(\theta\,t)v \,\dd \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} \ee^{\sca (\theta t-s) \Opgen} \Opgen v_{m+1} \delta_m( s)\,\dd s \,\dd \theta. \end{align*} With norm inequalities \tjnew{(note the nonexpansive case)} and Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we obtain \begin{align*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \,t\,\|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2 \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\dd s \,\dd \theta\\ &\leq \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m\, t^{m+1}\,\frac{1}{p!\,m!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta ^m\,\dd s \,\dd \theta\\ &= \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m \frac{t^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!}, \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{eresphijcor}. \tjnew{Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} is applied here in the nonexpansive case, see also the proof of Theorem \ref{theorem:upperboundexp}.}\hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Identify the leading term from the series, rewrite $L^{p,+}_m=\sca tAL^{p+1}_m$ as a double integral, then apply Proposition 3.1.

nodes.name: Identify the leading term
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: Applying~\eqref{em-phi-e1} (with $j=p+2$) to~\eqref{Lpplusleadingtermsum} shows~\eqref{leadingtermphijcor}: \begin{equation*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\, \gamma_m\, \frac{(\sca\,t)^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!} \,\Opgen v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+2}). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the asymptotics of $e_m^*\phif_{p+2}(\sca tT_m)e_1$ into the leading-term formula.

nodes.name: Rewrite as a double integral
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref{prop:generalSaadsum} we observe \begin{align*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \sigma\,t\,\Opgen \,\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v. \end{align*} Using the integral representation analogously as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi} for $L^{p+1}_m(t)v$ and formula~\eqref{LDint} for $L_m(t)v$, we obtain \begin{align*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v &= \sigma\,t\,\Opgen\,\, L^{p+1}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \Opgen\, L_m(\theta\,t)v \,\dd \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} \ee^{\sca (\theta t-s) \Opgen} \Opgen v_{m+1} \delta_m( s)\,\dd s \,\dd \theta. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Use $L^{p,+}_m=\sca tAL^{p+1}_m$ and the integral representations to express the error via $\delta_m$.

nodes.name: Apply norm inequalities and Proposition 3.1
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: With norm inequalities \tjnew{(note the nonexpansive case)} and Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we obtain \begin{align*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \,t\,\|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2 \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\dd s \,\dd \theta\\ &\leq \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m\, t^{m+1}\,\frac{1}{p!\,m!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta ^m\,\dd s \,\dd \theta\\ &= \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m \frac{t^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!}, \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{eresphijcor}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|\delta_m|$ by Proposition 3.1 and evaluate the resulting Beta integral.

nodes.name: Upper bounds via $\Erone$ for Hermitian $\sca\Opgen$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: \tjnew{For the nonexpansive case} with $\sca=1$ and \tjnew{a Hermitian} matrix $\Opgen$ we obtain \begin{equation*} |\delta_m(t)| = \delta_m(t) > 0 ~~~\text{for}~~t > 0. \end{equation*} This leads to the following upper bounds for the errors $L^p_m$ and $L^{p,+}_m$ with $p\geq 0$: \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \|L^p_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \, t \, \underbrace{e_m^\ast \, \phif_{p+1}(tT_m) \, e_1}_{\geq\, 0} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2 \,\tau_{m+1,m} \, t^2 \, \underbrace{e_m^\ast \, \phif_{p+2}(tT_m) \, e_1}_{\geq\, 0}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}
nodes.statement_short: For Hermitian $A$ with $\sca=1$ one has $\delta_m(t)>0$, so the $\Erone$-type quantities are genuine upper bounds for $L^p_m$ and $L^{p,+}_m$.
assumptions: \tjnew{For the nonexpansive case} with $\sca=1$ and \tjnew{a Hermitian} matrix $\Opgen$

nodes.name: Proof of the Hermitian upper bounds
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: For \tjnew{a Hermitian} matrix $\Opgen$ we obtain a symmetric, tridiagonal matrix $T_m$ with distinct, real eigenvalues via Lanczos approximation, see~\cite[Chap. 3.1]{horn85}. By Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we observe \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m \end{equation*} with $f_t(\lambda)=\ee^{t\,\lambda}$ for the case $\sca=1$. For divided differences of real-valued functions over real nodes we obtain $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \in \R$ and \begin{equation} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} = \frac{D^{(m-1)} f_t(\xi)}{(m-1)!} = \frac{t^{m-1} \ee^{t\xi}}{(m-1)!}~~~\text{for}~~\xi\in[\lambda_1,\lambda_m]. \end{equation} Equation~\eqref{ddreal} shows $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} > 0$ and with $\gamma_m > 0 $ we conclude \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) > 0,~~~\text{and}~~~|\delta_m(t)|=\delta_m(t). \end{equation*} We continue with~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1} in the case $p=0$: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)|\,\dd s = \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t e_m^\ast\,\ee^{sT_m} \,e_1 \,\dd s = \tau_{m+1,m} t \, e_m^\ast \, \phif_1(tT_m) \, e_1. \end{equation*} For the case $p \geq 1$ we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi}. Using definition~\eqref{defphiint} for the $\phif$-functions and resorting to the case $p=0$ we find \begin{align*} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\dd \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \phif_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\dd \theta. \end{align*} Evaluation of the integral yields \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \phif_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\dd \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p-1)!\,(k+1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^{k+1} \, \,\dd \theta \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p+k+1)!}\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,e_m^\ast \phif_{p+1}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1. \end{aligned} \end{equation} This shows~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1}. To show~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate2} we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:asymerrorpricorrected}: \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 = \|t\,\Opgen\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m} \,t\, \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\dd s \,\dd \theta. \end{equation*} Using $|\delta_m(s)|=\delta_m(s)$ and evaluating the inner integral by the $\phif_1$ function, we obtain \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,\frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \phif_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\dd \theta. \end{equation*} Evaluation of the integral analogously to~\eqref{partofproofphicor1}, \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,e_m^\ast \phif_{p+2}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1, \end{equation*} completes the proof. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Real divided differences give $\delta_m>0$; then treat $p=0$ directly and $p\ge1$ by the $\phif_p$ integral representation.

nodes.name: Positivity of $\delta_m(t)$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: For \tjnew{a Hermitian} matrix $\Opgen$ we obtain a symmetric, tridiagonal matrix $T_m$ with distinct, real eigenvalues via Lanczos approximation, see~\cite[Chap. 3.1]{horn85}. By Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we observe \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m \end{equation*} with $f_t(\lambda)=\ee^{t\,\lambda}$ for the case $\sca=1$. For divided differences of real-valued functions over real nodes we obtain $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \in \R$ and \begin{equation} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} = \frac{D^{(m-1)} f_t(\xi)}{(m-1)!} = \frac{t^{m-1} \ee^{t\xi}}{(m-1)!}~~~\text{for}~~\xi\in[\lambda_1,\lambda_m]. \end{equation} Equation~\eqref{ddreal} shows $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} > 0$ and with $\gamma_m > 0 $ we conclude \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) > 0,~~~\text{and}~~~|\delta_m(t)|=\delta_m(t). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Real nodes and a real function make the divided difference positive, hence $\delta_m(t)>0$.

nodes.name: Case $p=0$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: We continue with~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1} in the case $p=0$: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)|\,\dd s = \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t e_m^\ast\,\ee^{sT_m} \,e_1 \,\dd s = \tau_{m+1,m} t \, e_m^\ast \, \phif_1(tT_m) \, e_1. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate $\delta_m$ directly, recognising $\phif_1$.

nodes.name: Case $p\geq 1$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: For the case $p \geq 1$ we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi}. Using definition~\eqref{defphiint} for the $\phif$-functions and resorting to the case $p=0$ we find \begin{align*} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\dd \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \phif_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\dd \theta. \end{align*} Evaluation of the integral yields \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \phif_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\dd \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p-1)!\,(k+1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^{k+1} \, \,\dd \theta \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p+k+1)!}\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,e_m^\ast \phif_{p+1}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1. \end{aligned} \end{equation} This shows~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $p=0$ via the $\phif_p$ integral representation and sum the resulting series into $\phif_{p+1}$.

nodes.name: Bound for the corrected approximation
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and phi-functions
nodes.statement: To show~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate2} we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:asymerrorpricorrected}: \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 = \|t\,\Opgen\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m} \,t\, \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\dd s \,\dd \theta. \end{equation*} Using $|\delta_m(s)|=\delta_m(s)$ and evaluating the inner integral by the $\phif_1$ function, we obtain \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,\frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \phif_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\dd \theta. \end{equation*} Evaluation of the integral analogously to~\eqref{partofproofphicor1}, \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|\Opgen v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,e_m^\ast \phif_{p+2}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1, \end{equation*} completes the proof. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the argument for $L^{p,+}_m$, evaluating the inner integral by $\phif_1$.

nodes.name: Hermite quadrature approximation of the error integral
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement: \wa{To this end we again proceed from the integral representation~\eqref{LDint}, \begin{equation} L_m(t)v = \int_0^t \underbrace{E(t-s)\,D_m(s)}_{=:\;\Theta_m(s,t)}v\,\dd s. \end{equation} Due to $ \| D_m(t)v \| = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m-1}) $, \begin{equation*} \tfrac{\dd^j}{\dd\,s^j}\,D_m(s)v\big|_{s=0} = 0, \quad j=0,\ldots,m-2, \end{equation*} and the same is true for the integrand in~\eqref{LDint-1}, \begin{equation*} \tfrac{\partial^j}{\partial s^j}\,\Theta_m(s,t)v\big|_{s=0} = 0, \quad j=0,\ldots,m-2. \end{equation*} Analogously as in~\cite{auzingeretal13a}, this allows us to approximate~\eqref{LDint-1} by \tjnew{a Hermite quadrature} formula in the form \begin{equation} \int_0^t \Theta_m(s,t)v\,\dd s \approx \frac{t}{m}\,\Theta_m(t,t)v = \frac{t}{m}\,D_m(t)v. \end{equation} From~\eqref{Dm-lead}, \begin{equation*} \frac{t}{m}\,D_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\frac{(\sigma t)^{m}}{m!}\,v_{m+1} + {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}), \end{equation*} which is the same as~\eqref{asy-leading}. This means that the quadrature approximation~\eqref{LDint-1-appr} approximates the leading error term in an asymptotically correct way. } From~\eqref{LDint-1-appr},~\eqref{Dm(s)v} and~\eqref{defdelta} we obtain \begin{equation} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \approx \tau_{m+1,m}\frac{t}{m}|\delta_m(t)|. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Because the integrand vanishes to order $m-1$ at $s=0$, Hermite quadrature gives $L_m(t)v\approx (t/m)D_m(t)v$, which is asymptotically correct.

nodes.name: Order of the Hermite quadrature error and an improved quadrature estimate
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement: \wa{ The quadrature error in~\eqref{LDint-1-appr} is $ {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}) $. It is useful to argue this also in a direct way: By construction, the Hermite quadrature formula underlying~\eqref{LDint-1-appr} is of order~$ m $, and its error has the Peano representation (cf. also~\cite{auzingeretal13a}) \begin{equation} \frac{t}{m}\,\Theta_m(t,t) - \int_0^t \Theta_m(s,t)v\,\dd s = \int_0^t \frac{s\,(t-s)^{m-1}}{m!}\, \tfrac{\partial^{m}}{\partial s^{m}}\,\Theta_m(s,t)v\,\dd s. \end{equation} Here, $ \tfrac{\partial^{m}}{\partial s^{m}}\,\Theta_m(s,t)v = {\mathcal{O}}(1) $, because $ \tfrac{\dd^{m}}{\dd s^{m}}\,D_m(s)v = {\mathcal{O}}(1) $ which follows from $ D_m(s)v = {\mathcal{O}}(s^{m-1}) $. This shows that, indeed, the quadrature error~\eqref{quad-peano} is $ {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}) $. Furthermore, a quadrature formula of order $ m+1 $ can be constructed by including an additional evaluation of \begin{equation*} \tfrac{\partial}{\partial s}\,\Theta_m(s,t)v\big|_{s=t} = D_m^{[2]}(t)v, \quad \text{with} \quad D_m^{[2]}(t) = \tfrac{\dd}{\dd t} D_m(t) - \sca A\,D_m(t). \end{equation*} A routine calculation shows \begin{equation} \int_0^t \Theta_m(s,t)v\,\dd s = \frac{2\,t}{m+1}\,D_m(t)v - \frac{t^2}{m(m+1)}\,D_m^{[2]}(t)v + {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+2}), \end{equation} where the error depends on $ \tfrac{\dd^{m+1}}{\dd s^{m+1}}\,D_m(s)v = {\mathcal{O}}(1) $. This may be considered as an improved error estimate\footnote{In the setting of~\cite{auzingeretal13a} (higher-order splitting methods) such an improved error estimate was not taken into account since it cannot be evaluated with reasonable effort in that context.} which can be evaluated using \begin{equation*} \tfrac{\dd}{\dd t} D_m(t)v = \sca^2 \tau_{m+1,m}\,e_m^\ast(T_m\,\ee^{\sca\,t\,T_m})e_1 v_{m+1}. \end{equation*} With the solution in the Krylov subspace, $\ee^{\sca\,t\,T_m} e_1$ with $e_m^\ast \ee^{\sca\,t\,T_m} e_1 = (\ee^{\sca\,t\,T_m} e_1)_m$, we can compute the derivative of the defect at $\mathcal{O}(1)$ cost, \begin{align*} \tfrac{\dd}{\dd t} D_m(t)v &= \sca^2 \tau_{m+1,m}\,e_m^\ast(T_m\,\ee^{\sca\,t\,T_m})e_1 v_{m+1} \\ &= \sca^2 \tau_{m+1,m}\,\big((T_m)_{m,m}\, (\ee^{\sca\,t\,T_m} e_1)_m + (T_m)_{m,m-1}\, (\ee^{\sca\,t\,T_m} e_1)_{m-1}\big)v_{m+1}. \end{align*} Also longer expansions may be considered, for instance \begin{align*} &\int_0^t \Theta_m(s,t)v\,\dd s = \frac{3\,t}{m+2}\,D_m(t)v - \frac{3\,t^2}{(m+1)(m+2)}\,D_m^{[2]}(t)v \\ & \qquad\qquad {} + \frac{t^3}{m(m+1)(m+2)}\,D_m^{[3]}(t)v + {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+3}), \quad \text{with} \quad D_m^{[3]}(t) = \tfrac{\dd}{\dd t} D_m^{[2]}(t) - A\,D_m^{[2]}(t), \end{align*} etc. } \wa{This alternative way of computing improved error estimates is worth investigating but will not be pursued further here.}
nodes.statement_short: A Peano representation shows the quadrature error is $\mathcal{O}(t^{m+1})$; adding a defect-derivative term raises the order to $m+1$.

nodes.name: Trapezoidal rule error estimate
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement: In~\cite{lubich08} it is suggested to use the trapezoidal rule as a practical approximation to the integral~\eqref{errorapprox1}, \begin{equation} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)| \, \dd s \approx \tau_{m+1,m} \tfrac{t}{2} \,|\delta_m(t)|, \end{equation} or alternatively the Simpson rule.

nodes.name: Effective order $\rho(t)$
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement: The effective order of the function $ f(t) $ can be understood as the slope of the double-logarithmic function \begin{align*} &\xi(\tau)=\ln(f(\ee^{\tau}))~~~\text{with}~~\tau=\ln t, \\ \text{with derivative} \quad &\xi'(\tau)=\frac{f'(\ee^{\tau})\,\ee^{\tau}}{f(\ee^{\tau})}. \end{align*} We denote the order by \begin{equation} \rho(t)=\frac{f'(t)\,t}{f(t)}, \end{equation} and obtain \begin{equation*} f(t)=\frac{f'(t)\,t}{\rho(t)}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The effective order is the local slope of the double-logarithmic plot of $|\delta_m(t)|$, i.e. $\rho(t)=f'(t)t/f(t)$.

nodes.name: Bounds on the defect integral via the effective order
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement: Integration and application of the mean value theorem shows the existence of $t^\ast\in[0,t]$ with \begin{equation*} \int_0^t f(s)\,\dd s= \frac{1}{\rho(t^\ast)} \int_0^t f'(s)\,s\,\dd s, \end{equation*} and integration by parts gives \begin{equation*} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)| \,\dd s = \frac{t\, |\delta_m(t)|}{1+\rho(t^\ast)}. \end{equation*} With the plausible assumption that the order is bounded by $1\leq \tilde{m}\leq \rho(t) \leq m-1 =\rho(0+)$ for $t\in[0,T]$, we obtain \begin{equation} \tfrac{t}{m}\,|\delta_m(t)| \leq \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)| \,\dd s \leq \tfrac{t}{\tilde{m}+1}\,|\delta_m(t)| \leq \tfrac{t}{2}\,|\delta_m(t)|. \end{equation} The inequalities~\eqref{defintbounds} show that the error estimate based on the trapezoidal quadrature~\eqref{luquadtrapez} leads to an upper bound of the error. The error estimate based on Hermite quadrature \eqref{eq:hermitquadnorm} leads to a lower bound of the integral~\eqref{errorapprox1}, which not necessarily leads to a lower bound for the norm of the error. \tjnew{In contrast to~\eqref{eq:hermitquadnorm}, the error estimate~\eqref{luquadtrapez} is not asymptotically correct for $ t \to 0 $.}
nodes.statement_short: Under $1\le\tilde m\le\rho(t)\le m-1$ the defect integral is squeezed between $(t/m)|\delta_m(t)|$ and $(t/2)|\delta_m(t)|$, so the trapezoidal estimate is an upper bound.
assumptions: With the plausible assumption that the order is bounded by $1\leq \tilde{m}\leq \rho(t) \leq m-1 =\rho(0+)$ for $t\in[0,T]$

nodes.name: Effective order quadrature estimate
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement: With $\rho(0+)=m-1$ and the assumptions that the effective order is slowly decreasing locally at $t=0$ and sufficiently smooth, we suggest choosing $\tilde{m}=\rho(t)$ for a step of size $t$ \tjnew{to} improve the quadrature based estimate. \begin{equation} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)| \, \dd s \approx \tau_{m+1,m} \tfrac{t}{\rho(t)+1} \,|\delta_m(t)|, \end{equation} We will refer to this as \emph{effective order quadrature} estimate. In the limit $t\to0$ this choice of quadrature is equivalent to the Hermite quadrature and, therefore, asymptotically correct.
nodes.statement_short: Choosing $\tilde m=\rho(t)$ yields the effective order quadrature estimate $\tau_{m+1,m}t|\delta_m(t)|/(\rho(t)+1)$.

nodes.name: Onset of superlinear convergence
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: We recall from~\cite{hoclub97} that superlinear convergence as a function of $ m $, the dimension of the underlying Krylov space, sets in for \begin{equation} t\, \|\Opgen\|_2 \lessapprox m. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Restarted Krylov time propagation
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: We split the time range $[0,t]$ into $N$ subintervals, \begin{align*} 0&=t_0<t_1<\ldots<t_N=t, \\ \text{with step sizes}~~\Delta t_j&= t_{j}-t_{j-1},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{align*} The exact solution at time $t_j$ is denoted by $ \mv{j} $, whence \begin{equation*} \mv{j} = E(\Delta t_{j})\mv{j-1}=E(t_{j})v,\quad\text{with}\quad \mv{0}=v. \end{equation*} For simplicity we assume that the dimension $m$ of the Krylov subspace is fixed over the substeps. We obtain approximations $ \mw{j }$ to $ \mv{j} $ by applying multiple restarted Krylov steps, with orthonormal bases $ \Vmj $ and upper Hessenberg matrices $ \Tmj $. Starting from $ \mw{0} = v $, for $ j=1,\ldots,N $, \begin{align*} \mw{j} := \Smj(\Delta t_{j}) \mw{j-1} = \Vmj \ee^{\sca\,\Delta t_{j} \Tmj} \big(\Vmj\big)^\ast \mw{j-1} = \Vmj \ee^{\sca\,\Delta t_{j} \Tmj}e_1. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Split $[0,t]$ into substeps and propagate with a fresh $m$-dimensional Krylov approximation on each substep.
input: the dimension $m$ of the Krylov subspace is fixed over the substeps

nodes.name: Partition the time interval
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: We split the time range $[0,t]$ into $N$ subintervals, \begin{align*} 0&=t_0<t_1<\ldots<t_N=t, \\ \text{with step sizes}~~\Delta t_j&= t_{j}-t_{j-1},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Choose the grid $0=t_0<\ldots<t_N=t$ and the corresponding step sizes.

nodes.name: Propagate over each substep
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: Starting from $ \mw{0} = v $, for $ j=1,\ldots,N $, \begin{align*} \mw{j} := \Smj(\Delta t_{j}) \mw{j-1} = \Vmj \ee^{\sca\,\Delta t_{j} \Tmj} \big(\Vmj\big)^\ast \mw{j-1} = \Vmj \ee^{\sca\,\Delta t_{j} \Tmj}e_1. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Build a new Krylov basis at each substep and advance $\mw{j-1}\mapsto\mw{j}$.

nodes.name: Accumulated error $L_m^{\star}(t)v$
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: The error matrix in the $j$-th step is denoted by \begin{equation*} \Lmj(\Delta t_{j}) := E(\Delta t_{j})-\Smj(\Delta t_{j}), \end{equation*} and the accumulated error by \begin{equation} L_m^{\star}(t)v=\mv{N}-\mw{N}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Accumulated error bound for the restarted scheme
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: Recall our premise that $E(\cdot)$ is \wa{nonexpansive} and assume that the local error is bounded by \begin{equation} \|\Lmj(\Delta t_j)\mw{j}\|_2 \leq \ttol \cdot \Delta t_j. \end{equation} Then, \begin{equation*} \|L_m^{\star}(t)v\|_2 \leq \sum_{j=1}^N \|\Lmj(\Delta t_j) \mw{j-1}\|_2 \leq \ttol \sum_{j=1}^N \Delta t_j = \ttol \cdot t. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: If each local error obeys $\|\Lmj(\Delta t_j)\mw{j}\|_2\le\ttol\,\Delta t_j$, the accumulated error is at most $\ttol\cdot t$.

nodes.name: Step size selection based on $\Era$
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: For a single substep, the error estimate~\eqref{errornew} suggests a step size to satisfy a given error tolerance $\ttol$ as \begin{equation} \Delta t_j = \left(\frac{\ttol\, \, m!}{\tau^{[j]}_{m+1,m}\gamma^{[j]}_m}\right)^{1/m},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{equation} For a local error as in~\eqref{localerror}, we replace $\ttol$ by $ (\Delta t_j\,\,\ttol)$ in~\eqref{choosestepbyEra} and obtain \begin{equation} \Delta t_j = \left(\frac{\ttol\, \, m!}{\tau^{[j]}_{m+1,m}\gamma^{[j]}_m}\right)^{1/(m-1)},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Inverting the $\Era$ bound gives an explicit step size for a prescribed tolerance, with exponent $1/m$ (global) or $1/(m-1)$ (local).

nodes.name: Step size for the corrected Krylov approximation
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: For the corrected Krylov approximation $\Scor_m(t)\mv{j}$, see~\eqref{Smbar}, the error estimate given in~\eqref{eresphijcor} ($p=0$) suggests a local step size of \begin{equation} \Delta t_j = \left(\frac{\ttol\, \, (m+1)!}{\big\|\Opgen\mvmone{j}\big\|_2\,\tau^{[j]}_{m+1,m}\gamma^{[j]}_m}\right)^{1/m},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Heuristic step size control
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: For a step, with step size $\Delta t_{j-1}$ and estimated error $\Er^{[j-1]}$, a reasonable size for the subsequent step can be chosen as \begin{equation} \Delta t_{j} = \left( \frac{\tjnew{\Delta t_{j}}\,\,\ttol}{\Er^{[j-1]}}\right)^{1/m} \Delta t_{j-1},\quad j=2,\ldots,N. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The next step size is extrapolated from the previous one and its measured error estimate.

nodes.name: Expokit a priori first step size
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: The first step size in~\cite{sidje98} is chosen as \begin{equation} \Delta t_1 = \frac{1}{\|H\|_{\infty}}\,\left(\frac{\ttol\,\, ((m+1)/\ee)^{m+1}\sqrt{2\,\pi\,(m+1)}}{4\,\|H\|_{\infty}}\right)^{1/m}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Iterative step size adaptation for Hermitian $\Opgen$
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: In the case of a Hermitian matrix $\Opgen$ the matrix $T_m$ is symmetric, tridiagonal and real-valued which allows cheap and robust computation of its eigenvalue decomposition. The eigenvalue decomposition of $T_m$ is independent of the step size $\Delta t$ and allows cheap evaluation of $\Erone$ for multiple choices of $\Delta t$. In this case we can cheaply adapt the choice of $\Delta t_j$ in an iterative manner before continuing to time step $j+1$: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \Delta t_{j,1}&:= \Delta t_{j-1}~~\text{or result of~\eqref{choosestepbyEralocal}},\\ \Delta t_{j,l}&:= \Big( \frac{\tjnew{\Delta t_{j,l}}\,\,\ttol}{\Er^{[j,l-1]}}\Big)^{1/m} \Delta t_{j,l-1},~~~~~ l=2,\ldots,N_j,\\ \Delta t_{j}&:=\Delta t_{j,N_j}.\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} By choosing $\Er^{[j,l-1]}$ as an error estimate for the Krylov approximation of the $j$-th step with time step $\Delta t_{j,l-1}$. For $\Er^{[j,l-1]}$ we can use $\Erone$ or estimates given in Section~\ref{sec:defectquad}. The aim of the iteration~\eqref{eq:stepsize2loops} is to determine a step size $\Delta t_{j,\infty}$ with $\Er^{[j,\infty]}=\ttol$. The convergence behavior of iteration~\eqref{eq:stepsize2loops} depends on the structure of the corresponding error estimate. In our practical examples this iteration converges monotonically in a small number of steps. This step size iteration can also be used for the case of non-Hermitian $\Opgen$ with the drawback of higher computational cost for the error estimate $\Er^{[j,l-1]}$ for every $j$ and $l$.
nodes.statement_short: A cheap eigendecomposition of $T_m$ allows $\Erone$ to be re-evaluated for many trial step sizes, enabling an inner step-size iteration.

nodes.name: Iterative step size adaptation
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: In this case we can cheaply adapt the choice of $\Delta t_j$ in an iterative manner before continuing to time step $j+1$: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \Delta t_{j,1}&:= \Delta t_{j-1}~~\text{or result of~\eqref{choosestepbyEralocal}},\\ \Delta t_{j,l}&:= \Big( \frac{\tjnew{\Delta t_{j,l}}\,\,\ttol}{\Er^{[j,l-1]}}\Big)^{1/m} \Delta t_{j,l-1},~~~~~ l=2,\ldots,N_j,\\ \Delta t_{j}&:=\Delta t_{j,N_j}.\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the heuristic step-size formula within a single step until the estimated error matches the tolerance.
input: $\Er^{[j,l-1]}$ as an error estimate for the Krylov approximation of the $j$-th step with time step $\Delta t_{j,l-1}$

nodes.name: Initialize the trial step size
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: \Delta t_{j,1}&:= \Delta t_{j-1}~~\text{or result of~\eqref{choosestepbyEralocal}},\\
nodes.statement_short: Start from the previous step size or from the asymptotic formula.

nodes.name: Iterate the heuristic update
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: \Delta t_{j,l}&:= \Big( \frac{\tjnew{\Delta t_{j,l}}\,\,\ttol}{\Er^{[j,l-1]}}\Big)^{1/m} \Delta t_{j,l-1},~~~~~ l=2,\ldots,N_j,\\
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly rescale the step size by the ratio of tolerance to estimated error.

nodes.name: Return the accepted step size
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator
nodes.statement: \Delta t_{j}&:=\Delta t_{j,N_j}.\\
nodes.statement_short: Return $\Delta t_{j,N_j}$.

nodes.name: Free Schr{\"o}dinger equation
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case
nodes.statement: We consider \begin{equation} H=\tfrac{1}{4}\, \text{tridiag}(-1,2,-1) \in\R^{n\times n}, \end{equation} with dimension $n=10\,000$. The matrix $H$ is \tjnew{associated with a finite difference or finite element discretization of the one-dimensional negative Laplacian}. With $A=H$ and $\sca=-\ii$, in~\eqref{exp(itA)v} we obtain the free Schr{\"o}dinger equation. The eigenvalue decomposition of $H$ is well known, and we can use the discrete sine transform with high precision arithmetic in Matlab to compute the exact solution $E(t)v$, see~\eqref{exp(itA)v}. The starting vector $v$ is chosen randomly. To compute the Krylov subspace approximation $S_m(t)v$, see \eqref{Smv}, we use the eigenvalue decomposition of the tridiagonal matrix $T_m$.
nodes.statement_short: A $10\,000\times10\,000$ discrete one-dimensional Laplacian with $\sca=-\ii$, giving the free Schr{\"o}dinger propagator.

nodes.name: Discrete Hubbard model
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case
nodes.statement:
For the description of the Hubbard model we employ a self-contained notation. The Hubbard model first appears in~\cite{hubbard63} and was further used in many papers and books, e.g.~\cite{Ma93,PKBS16}. The Hubbard model is used to describe electron density on a given number of sites, which correspond to Wannier discretization of orbitals, and spin up or down. We consider the following Hubbard Hamiltonian, in second quantization and without chemical potential:  egin{equation} H= rac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j,\sigma} v_{ij} c_{j\sigma}^{\dagger} c_{i\sigma} + \sum_{j,\sigma} U \hat{n}_{j\sigma}\hat{n}_{j\sigma'}, \end{equation} where $i,j$ sum over the number of sites $
sit$ and the spins $\sigma,\sigma' \in\{\uparrow,\downarrow \}$ where $\sigma'$ is the opposite spin to $\sigma$. The entries $v_{ij}$ with $i,j=1,\ldots,
sit$ describe electron hopping from site $i$ to $j$. In~\eqref{eq.HubHam}, the notation $c_{j\sigma}^\dagger c_{i\sigma}$ describes the $2$nd quantization operator and $\hat{n}_{j\sigma}=c_{j\sigma}^\dagger c_{j\sigma}$ the occupation number operator. For details on the notation in~\eqref{eq.HubHam} we can recommend several references, e.g.~\cite{hubbard63,Ja08,Ma93,PKBS16}. For our tests we model $8$ electrons at $8$ sites ($
sit=8$) with spin up and down for each site, this leads to $16$ possible states for electrons. Such an electron distribution is also referred to as half-filled in the literature. We also restrict our model by considering the number of electrons with spin up and down to be fixed as $
sit/2$. This leads to $n=(	ext{binomial}(8,4))^2=4900$ considered occupation states which create a discrete basis. For the numerical implementation of the basis we consider $16$-bit integers for which each bit describes a position which is occupied in case the bit is equal to $1$ or empty otherwise. The set of occupation states can be ordered by the value of the integers which leads to a unique representation of the Hubbard Hamiltonian~\eqref{eq.HubHam} by a matrix $H\in\C^{n	imes n}$. Such an implementation of the Hubbard Hamiltonian is also described in~\cite[Section 3]{Ja08}. In our test setting we use $U=5$ and parameter-dependent values for electron hopping $v_{ij}=v_{ij}(\omega)\in\C$ with $\omega\in(0,2\pi]$:  egin{align*} &v_{11}=v_{88}=-1.75,~~~v_{jj}=-2~~	ext{for}~~j=2,\ldots,7,\ &v_{j,j+1}= ar{v}_{j+1,j}=-\cos\omega+\ii\,\sin\omega~~	ext{for}~~j=1,\ldots,7~~	ext{and}~~v_{ij}=0~~~	ext{otherwise}. \end{align*} For this choice of $v_{ij}(\omega)$ we obtain 	jnew{a Hermitian} matrix $H_\omega\in\C^{n	imes n}$ with $43980$ nonzero entries (for a general choice of $\omega$) and $	ext{spec}(H_\omega)\subseteq (-19.1,8.3)$. The spectrum of $H_\omega$ is independent of $\omega$. A relevant application where the Hubbard Hamiltonian~\eqref{eq.HubHam} is of importance is the simulation of oxide solar cells with the goal of finding candidates for new materials promising a gain in the efficiency of the solar cell, see~\cite{Held2007}. The study of solar cells considers time-dependent electron hoppings $v_{ij}=v_{ij}(t)$ to model time-dependent potentials which lead to Hamiltonian matrices $H(t)$. 	jnew{The time-dependent Hamiltonian can be parameterized via~$\omega$.} Time propagation of a linear, non-autonomous ODE system can be approximated by Magnus-type integrators which are based on one or more evaluations of matrix exponentials applied to different starting vectors at several times $ t $, see 	jnew{for instance~\cite{blanesetal08b,blamoa05}}. Our test setting for the Hubbard Hamiltonian with arbitrary $\omega$ is then obtained by~\eqref{exp(itA)v} with the matrix $A=H_\omega$ as described above and $\sca=-\ii$.
nodes.statement_short: A half-filled 8-site Hubbard Hamiltonian ($n=4900$, $U=5$, $\omega$-dependent hopping) used as a skew-Hermitian test problem.

nodes.name: Numerical verification of the upper error bound
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case
nodes.statement: We observe that the error estimate $\Erone$ is a good approximation \tjnew{to the error}, but it is not an upper bound in general. In contrast, $\Era$ is a \tjnew{proven} upper error bound. Up to round-off error, for $m=10$ we observe the correct asymptotic behavior of $\Era$ and $\Erone$. For larger choices of $m$ the asymptotic regime starts at time steps for which the error is already close to round-off precision. Therefore, for larger choices of $m$, the Krylov approximation, as a time integrator, cannot achieve its full order for typical time steps in double precision.
nodes.statement_short: $\Erone$ tracks the error well but is not an upper bound, whereas $\Era$ is; for large $m$ the asymptotic regime is masked by round-off.
conclusions: We observe that the error estimate $\Erone$ is a good approximation \tjnew{to the error}, but it is not an upper bound in general. In contrast, $\Era$ is a \tjnew{proven} upper error bound.

nodes.name: Mass conservation of the standard Krylov approximation
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case
nodes.statement: In exact arithmetic we obtain mass conservation for the skew-Hermitian case: For the case $\|v\|_2=1$ and standard Krylov approximation $S_m(t)v$ we have \begin{equation} \|S_m(t)v\|_2 = \|V_m \ee^{-\ii\,t\,T_m}e_1\|_2 = e_1^\ast \ee^{\ii\,t\,T_m} V_m^\ast V_m\ee^{-\ii\,t\,T_m}e_1=1. \end{equation} The requirement $V_m^\ast V_m=I$ is essential to obtain mass conservation in~\eqref{eq:massconsv}.
nodes.statement_short: In exact arithmetic the skew-Hermitian standard Krylov approximation preserves $\|S_m(t)v\|_2=1$, provided $V_m^*V_m=I$.
assumptions: For the case $\|v\|_2=1$ and standard Krylov approximation $S_m(t)v$

nodes.name: Rounding of step sizes in Expokit
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case
nodes.statement: In the Expokit code the step sizes are rounded to $2$ digits in every step. Rounding the step size can give too large errors in some steps. This makes it necessary to include safety parameters in Expokit which on the other hand slow down the performance of the code. It seems advisable to avoid any kind of rounding of step sizes.
nodes.statement_short: Rounding step sizes forces safety factors that slow the code down; it is better avoided.

nodes.name: Cheap versus expensive error estimates
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case
nodes.statement: Error estimates for the corrected Krylov approximation or improved error estimates such as the improved Hermite quadrature~\eqref{eq:improvedHermiteQuad} require additional matrix-vector multiplications. Instead of investing computational effort in improving the error estimate, one may as well increase the dimension of the standard Krylov subspace. For comparison we test the original Expokit code, the corrected Krylov approximation with error estimate $\Era^+$ and the improved Hermite quadrature~\eqref{eq:improvedHermiteQuad} with Krylov subspace $m-1$. Table~\ref{Table:ExpensivErrEstvsCheapErrEst} shows that a standard Krylov approximation with dimension $m$ leads to better results, although all considered versions use the same number of matrix-vector multiplications. Since the reliability of error estimates such as $\Era$ has been demonstrated earlier, it appears that additional cost to improve the error estimate is not justified.
nodes.statement_short: At equal matrix-vector cost, enlarging the standard Krylov subspace beats spending effort on a better error estimate.

nodes.name: Heat equation
nodes.section: 8.2 The Hermitian case
nodes.statement: \tjnew{ \paragraph{Heat equation.} To obtain the heat equation in~\eqref{exp(itA)v} we choose $A=H$ in~\eqref{Hschroe} and $\sca=-1$. Details on the test setting are already given in Subsection~\ref{sec:skew-herm}.} For the heat equation, $H$ given in~\eqref{Hschroe}, we can also verify the error estimates, see Figure~\ref{fig:numexheat}. In comparison to the skew-Hermitian case we do not observe a large time regime for which the error is of the asymptotic order $m$. As shown in Proposition~\ref{upperboundphi} we do obtain \tjnew{an upper error bound} using $\Erone$ for the heat equation. However, the evolution is not unitary but nonexpansive in this case, whence the asymptotics are not observed as clearly here.
nodes.statement_short: The same tridiagonal $H$ with $\sca=-1$ gives a Hermitian (parabolic) test problem where the asymptotic order is less visible.

nodes.name: Convection-diffusion problem
nodes.section: 8.3 A non-normal problem
nodes.statement: For a more general case we consider a convection-diffusion equation (see \cite{MN01,EE06}). \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\partial_t u = \Delta u - \tau_1 \partial_{x_1} u - \tau_2 \partial_{x_2} u,~~\tau_1,\tau_2\in\R,~~~u=u(t,x),~~t\geq 0,~~ x\in\Omega=[0,1]^3,\\ &u(0,x)=v(x)~~\text{for}~x\in\Omega,~~u(t,x)=0~~\text{for}~x\in\partial\Omega. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Following \cite{MN01,EE06} we use a central finite difference scheme to discretize the partial differential operator in~\eqref{convdifpde}. The grid is chosen uniformly with $(n+2)^3$ points and mesh width $h=1/(n+1)$. The dimension $N$ of the discrete operator is $N=n^3$. Choosing $n=15$ we obtain $N=3357$. The discretized operator is given by \begin{align} &A=( I_{n\times n} \otimes (I_{n\times n} \otimes C_1) ) + ( B \otimes I_{n\times n} + I_{n\times n}\otimes C_2 ) \otimes I_{n\times n} )\in\R^{N\times N},~~~\text{with}\\ &~~~B=\tfrac{1}{h^2} \text{tridiag}(1,-2,1)\in\R^n,~~~ C_i=\tfrac{1}{h^2} \text{tridiag}(1+\mu_i,-2,1-\mu_i)\in\R^n,~~i=1,2,\notag \end{align} and $\mu_i=\tau_i\,(h/2)$. The spectrum of the non-normal matrix $A$ in~\eqref{Aconvdif} (see \cite{MN01}) satisfies \begin{align*} \text{spec}(A)\subseteq &\tfrac{1}{h^2}\,[-6-2\cos(\pi\,h)\text{Re}(\theta),-6+2\cos(\pi\,h)\text{Re}(\theta)] \\ &~\times \tfrac{1}{h^2}\,\ii\,[-2\cos(\pi\,h)\text{Im}(\theta),2\cos(\pi\,h)\text{Im}(\theta)] . \end{align*} with $\theta = 1 + \sqrt{1-\mu_1^2} + \sqrt{1-\mu_2^2}$. Therefore, the eigenvalues are complex-valued if at least one $\mu_i>1$. The matrix $A$ depends on the parameters $\mu_i$, correspondingly $\tau_i$, for which we consider two different cases, \begin{equation} \text{$\mu_1=0.9$, $\mu_2=1.1$},~~~\text{with}~~\text{spec}(h^2\,A) \subseteq [-9,-3] \times \ii[-1,1], \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \text{$\mu_1=\mu_2=10$},~~~\text{with}~~\text{spec}(h^2\,A) \subseteq [-8,-4] \times \ii [ -39,39]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A central-difference discretization of a 3D convection-diffusion operator ($N=3357$) giving a non-normal test matrix in two parameter regimes.
